not_on_paper.why: Keeping a spelling log and checking words in a dictionary or on screen is a habit built over weeks, not an answer on one paper.
not_on_paper.observe: Look at the child's spelling log once a fortnight: are misspelt words from their writing added, practised and ticked off?

not_on_paper.why: Using a word list, dictionary or thesaurus to widen the words in their writing shows only across a run of written work.
not_on_paper.observe: Compare two pieces of writing a month apart: has the child used words from their own word list or a thesaurus?

not_on_paper.reason: range of reading over a term
not_on_paper.why: Reading and exploring many kinds of fiction, poems and playscripts is about how widely a child reads across a term.
not_on_paper.observe: Keep the reading record: by the end of term has the child read a story, a poem and a playscript, and talked about a picture in one?

not_on_paper.reason: range of reading over a term
not_on_paper.why: Reading many kinds of non-fiction is about the range a child meets over a term, not one passage.
not_on_paper.observe: Keep the reading record: has the child read instructions, a report and a recount this term, in class or at home?

not_on_paper.why: Enjoying reading alone and with others is seen in how a child chooses and talks about books, not in marks.
not_on_paper.observe: During Reading Time, note whether the child chooses books freely, stays with them and asks to share them.

not_on_paper.why: Reading silently can only be watched: whether the child reads without saying the words aloud and keeps their place.
not_on_paper.observe: During silent reading, watch for lip movement and finger pointing, then ask one question about the page.

not_on_paper.why: Creative writing in many kinds of story and poem is a full piece over a lesson or more, judged across the term.
not_on_paper.observe: Use the exercise-book pieces from Storybook, Mind Pictures and Poems to Ponder; judge them with the writing rubric.

not_on_paper.why: Writing a whole text for a purpose with the features of its type needs a full piece, not a few lines.
not_on_paper.observe: Use the information page from Going Deep and the instructions from Food for Thought; check the features of each type.

not_on_paper.why: Choosing content and language for a named reader shows in a full piece written for that reader.
not_on_paper.observe: Use an advert or invitation written in class for a named reader; ask: would that reader understand and want to read it?

not_on_paper.why: Legible, fluent joined handwriting is judged across exercise books, not from one answer.
not_on_paper.observe: Look at one page of the exercise book each half-term: are letters formed, sized and joined steadily?

not_on_paper.why: Choosing between handwritten, printed and on-screen layouts needs a screen and a real purpose, which a paper cannot give.
not_on_paper.observe: In a computing or class project, watch the child lay out a page on screen and say why they chose it.

not_on_paper.why: Speaking fluently and confidently is heard, not written.
not_on_paper.observe: In show-and-tell or a unit's speaking task, note whether the child speaks without long stops in familiar topics.

not_on_paper.why: Choosing the right information and detail when speaking is heard in talk.
not_on_paper.observe: Ask the child to tell a partner how to get to the library; note what they include and leave out.

not_on_paper.why: Choosing words to suit the situation is heard in talk.
not_on_paper.observe: Note the words the child uses with a friend and when speaking to the class or a visitor.

not_on_paper.why: Gesture, eye contact and expression are seen while a child speaks.
not_on_paper.observe: During a presentation, note eye contact, gesture and facial expression.

not_on_paper.why: Adapting language and tone to an audience is heard in talk.
not_on_paper.observe: Compare how the child speaks to younger children in a buddy reading session and to their class.

not_on_paper.why: Listening and following spoken instructions is shown in what the child does after hearing them.
not_on_paper.observe: Give three spoken steps (fold, colour, write); note whether the child carries out each in order.

not_on_paper.why: Asking questions about what was heard is spoken.
not_on_paper.observe: After a read-aloud, note whether the child's question is about a main point of what was read.

not_on_paper.why: Taking a role in a group is seen during group work.
not_on_paper.observe: In a group task, give roles (reader, writer, timekeeper) and note whether the child keeps theirs.

not_on_paper.why: Replying politely to another view is heard in discussion.
not_on_paper.observe: In a class discussion, note whether the child disagrees politely and gives their own view.

not_on_paper.why: Adding relevant comments to a discussion is heard in discussion.
not_on_paper.observe: In group talk, note whether the child's comments stay on the topic and move it on.

not_on_paper.why: Taking turns and acknowledging others is seen in discussion.
not_on_paper.observe: In group talk, note whether the child waits, listens and refers to what someone said.

not_on_paper.why: Reading aloud with expression is heard.
not_on_paper.observe: Listen to the child read a short passage aloud; note expression that fits the meaning.

not_on_paper.why: Using different voices when reading aloud is heard.
not_on_paper.observe: When the child reads a story with dialogue aloud, note whether characters sound different.

not_on_paper.why: Reading a familiar text aloud accurately, with its punctuation, is heard.
not_on_paper.observe: Listen to the child read a familiar page aloud; count words misread and pauses missed at full stops.

not_on_paper.why: Creating a character with voice, gesture and movement is a performance.
not_on_paper.observe: In the Let's Perform unit, watch the child play a character and note voice and movement.

not_on_paper.why: Planning and giving a presentation alone is a spoken performance.
not_on_paper.observe: Watch the child's presentation on a familiar subject; note its order and whether it was planned.

not_on_paper.why: Evaluating talk is done in talk, straight after it.
not_on_paper.observe: After presentations, ask the child to say one thing that went well and one to improve.

not_on_paper.why: Commenting on how meaning is shown with words and without them is a spoken reflection.
not_on_paper.observe: After a drama or presentation, ask how the speaker showed feeling without words.

not_on_paper.why: Keeping a spelling log and checking spellings with a dictionary or on screen is a habit built over weeks.
not_on_paper.observe: Look at the spelling log once a fortnight: are words from the child's own writing added, learnt and ticked off?

not_on_paper.why: Using a word list, dictionary or thesaurus to widen the words in writing shows only across a run of work.
not_on_paper.observe: Compare two pieces of writing a month apart for words taken from the child's word list or a thesaurus.

not_on_paper.reason: range of reading over a term
not_on_paper.why: Reading many kinds of fiction, poems and playscripts is about how widely a child reads across a term.
not_on_paper.observe: Keep the reading record: by the end of term, a novel chapter, a poem, a playscript, and a comment on a picture.

not_on_paper.reason: range of reading over a term
not_on_paper.why: Reading many kinds of non-fiction is about the range a child meets over a term.
not_on_paper.observe: Keep the reading record: a report, an advert, a recipe and a news article this term, in class or at home.

not_on_paper.why: Enjoying reading alone and with others is seen in how a child chooses and talks about books.
not_on_paper.observe: During Reading Time, note whether the child picks books freely, finishes them and asks to share them.

not_on_paper.why: Having favourite books and recommending them is shown in talk with others over time.
not_on_paper.observe: Once a half-term, ask the child to recommend a book to a friend and note whether they give a reason.

not_on_paper.why: Creative writing in many kinds of story and poem is a full piece over a lesson or more, judged across the term.
not_on_paper.observe: Use the exercise-book pieces from Storybook, Just Imagine and Poems to Ponder; judge them with the writing rubric.

not_on_paper.why: Writing a whole text for a purpose with the features of its type needs a full piece.
not_on_paper.observe: Use the information page from Going Deep and the advert from Food for Thought; check the features of each type.

not_on_paper.why: Choosing content and language for a named reader shows in a full piece written for that reader.
not_on_paper.observe: Use a letter or advert written in class for a named reader; ask whether that reader would understand it and be persuaded.

not_on_paper.why: Legible, fluent and quicker handwriting is judged across exercise books and timed writing.
not_on_paper.observe: Each half-term, time three minutes of copying and look at one page of the book for letter shape and joins.

not_on_paper.why: Choosing between handwritten, printed and on-screen layouts needs a screen and a purpose.
not_on_paper.observe: In a project, watch the child lay out a page on screen with headings and pictures and say why.

not_on_paper.why: Speaking accurately and at length is heard, not written.
not_on_paper.observe: In a unit's speaking task, note whether the child speaks for a minute or more with few errors.

not_on_paper.why: Putting information in an order that helps the listener is heard in talk.
not_on_paper.observe: Ask the child to explain a recipe to a partner; note whether the steps come in order.

not_on_paper.why: Choosing exact words when speaking is heard in talk.
not_on_paper.observe: Note whether the child uses precise words (sprinted, fragile) rather than general ones when explaining.

not_on_paper.why: Gesture, eye contact and expression are seen while a child speaks.
not_on_paper.observe: During a presentation, note eye contact, gesture and facial expression.

not_on_paper.why: Adapting language and tone to an audience is heard in talk.
not_on_paper.observe: Compare the child talking to a younger class during buddy reading and to a visitor.

not_on_paper.why: Listening, then asking and answering questions to build ideas, is spoken.
not_on_paper.observe: After a talk by a classmate, note whether the child's question builds on what was said.

not_on_paper.why: Taking a role in a group is seen during group work.
not_on_paper.observe: Give group roles and note whether the child keeps theirs to the end of the task.

not_on_paper.why: Replying politely to another view is heard in discussion.
not_on_paper.observe: In a class debate, note whether the child disagrees politely and gives a reason.

not_on_paper.why: Adding comments and questions that move a discussion on is heard.
not_on_paper.observe: In group talk, note comments and questions that stay on topic and add something new.

not_on_paper.why: Taking turns and building on others is seen in discussion.
not_on_paper.observe: In group talk, note whether the child links what they say to the speaker before.

not_on_paper.why: Reading aloud with expression, pace and volume is heard.
not_on_paper.observe: Listen to the child read a lively passage aloud; note changes of pace and volume.

not_on_paper.why: Reading aloud accurately and fluently with its punctuation is heard.
not_on_paper.observe: Listen to a page read aloud; count words misread and pauses missed at commas and full stops.

not_on_paper.why: Changing voice, gesture and movement to play a character is a performance.
not_on_paper.observe: In the Let's Perform unit, watch the child play a character and change it for another.

not_on_paper.why: Planning and giving a group presentation to a wider audience is a performance.
not_on_paper.observe: Watch the group's presentation in assembly; note the child's part in planning and speaking.

not_on_paper.why: Evaluating talk is done in talk, straight after it.
not_on_paper.observe: After presentations, ask the child for one strength and one change for next time.

not_on_paper.why: Commenting on how meaning is shown with words and without them is a spoken reflection.
not_on_paper.observe: After a drama, ask how a speaker's face and hands changed what their words meant.
